{"notes": "Visit 1 (left at 1:15). Only Sofia and Jack spoke. I did not see or hear Omar or Hana, so I have no evidence on them yet and will not guess. I'll check on them next visit and ask them privately what they're working on.

Sofia: Sketched the fish on the pad and defined the plan: stroke 1 is the top line, stroke 2 is the bottom line, and the tail flares at the right end. She took a tray of dominoes and started from the nose. She made a small swap with Jack, saying whoever traces stroke 1 lays the start domino, so she takes the top line. That was a sensible, clearly explained fix, though it reversed the split Jack had just agreed to. She also proposed checking tail ends and joins once both strokes are done, which is good quality thinking. Strong early signs for leadership and collaboration. Execution is plausible but not attributable.

Jack: Positive and agreeable. He praised the sketch, went to fetch 40 dominoes for the bin, and accepted the swap to stroke 2 (bottom line). He was away for most of this visit, so I have nothing on his building yet. Supplying the bin helps the team.

Table at 1:15: one connected chain runs from the START domino, up and to the right, about 10 dominoes with no visible gaps. It looks like the top line from the nose. The bottom line, tail flare and fins aren't started. I don't know who placed which domino, so I'm crediting no one for the chain beyond Sofia's stated intent to build it.

Open questions: Who is doing the tail and fins? Are Omar and Hana contributing? Is 10 dominoes in about 1:15 on pace for 10 minutes? Check the joins and the tail next visit."}

{"notes": "Visit 2 (left 2:45). Chain is now much further along: the top line runs connected from the nose to the up-flare at the tail, and the bottom line is connected from the fork to about x=25. The bottom-right flare (pale, around x=23-27, y=12-15.5) is NOT connected to the chain. It overlaps the bottom line's end, so it needs a join check. I still don't know who placed which domino, so I'm crediting only what people said and did in front of me, checked against the table.

Sofia: Said she's on the bottom line, and the connected bottom line matches that. She kept the roles clear (told Omar to stay off the bottom, asked him to watch the top tail, proposed meeting at the tail for join checks). Good leadership and collaboration. She now says Jack keeps the top, reversing her visit-1 plan where she took it. It's minor, but I'll ask if the handoff was agreed. Execution is likely solid but not directly seen.

Omar: First real evidence this visit and strong. At 2:00 he flagged a jammed domino at the fork, and the fork now connects. At 2:15 he carried the top line into the flare, offering to back off if Jack was already on it. Jack confirmed his help. Good impact, execution and collaboration, and he communicated clearly. No leadership signal beyond taking initiative.

Jack: Top tail finished (credited Omar). He offered to build the bottom flare and invited Sofia to take it, and asked Omar to review from the nose. Supportive and communicative. His flare is currently disconnected, so I'll check whether it gets joined.

Hana: Still nothing seen or heard in two visits. No rating evidence. I must ask her directly next visit what she's working on, and not guess.

Next: check the flare join, the tail ends and the overall alignment."}

{"notes": "Visit 3 (left 6:00). Key fact: the bottom flare (pale, x≈23-27, y≈11-15.5) is STILL not connected. The dark bottom line ends near x=23, y=11.5, and the flare begins just past it. If it stays open, none of the flare falls. Top line is connected nose to tail and looks fine.

Hana: First real evidence. At 5:00 she spotted Jack and Omar doubling up on the join, assigned Jack to finish it, told Omar to hold off, and proposed a group fall check from the nose. Clear, fair, well-timed coordination, a good leadership and collaboration signal. Still haven't seen her place or build anything, so impact and execution are unrated. Ask what she's building. 'Bin's still full' is unclear, so ask what she meant.

Jack: Cleared strays and took the join as assigned, and communicated. But he said 'closing the join now' at 5:15 and again at 5:45, and the gap was still open at 6:00. Twice asking Omar to stay clear may have held up the fix. Not yet a verdict; if it stays open that's an execution miss. Earlier: top tail finished, credited Omar.

Omar: Accepted the redirect gracefully, apologised, confirmed the patch was clear, and offered to close the join if it was still open with 1.5 minutes left. Good collaboration, reliable. Earlier fork fix and tail help still stand.

Sofia: Not seen this visit. Bottom line connected, which fits her role. Still need to ask about the top-line handoff to Jack.

Next: check the join first. If it is open, tell Jack to hand it to Omar or close it now. Then do the group fall check."}

{"notes": "Visit 4 (left 8:45). KEY FACT: the bottom flare (pale, x≈24-27, y≈11-15.5) is STILL disconnected. The dark bottom line ends near x=23.5, y=11.5 and the flare is still pale. About 1:15 left. Top line is connected and fine. If the join stays open, the flare won't fall. Next visit: check the join first, and don't take 'closing now' on trust.

Jack: At 7:45 he said 'bridge is down, quick look at the join, hang tight'. That is the third 'on it' update (5:15, 5:45, 7:45) with no visible result. I never saw him close it. Sofia stepped in at 8:00-8:15, so I suspect the join had stalled with him. Not a verdict, since I don't know what he did when I was away. Ask him what's catching. Communication is good, but execution on the join is a miss so far.

Sofia: Took initiative on the join. At 8:00 she gave a clear, fair fallback ('if still pale at 1:30 I'll redo it, you stay clear'). At 8:15 and 8:30 she said she was closing it and asked for space. Strong leadership and collaboration signal, and her bottom line is connected. But the picture still shows the gap open, so her execution is unproven. She also repeated 'closing now' twice with no visible result. Ask what's going wrong with the connect. Still need to ask about the top-line handoff to Jack.

Hana: Not seen this visit. Earlier, good coordination at 5:00. Still haven't seen her build, so impact and execution are unrated. Ask what she's building and what 'bin's still full' meant.

Omar: Not seen this visit. Earlier: graceful redirect, offered to close the join, fork fix and tail help. Reliable. Could be the fresh pair of hands for the join."}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I kept the table supplied so the builders never had to stop for dominoes. I fetched three full loads of 40 for the shared bin, at about 0:45, 1:45 and 3:00, so the bin was stocked through the whole build. That let Sofia, Jack and Omar lay the top line, bottom line, and tail flares without running dry. The fish outline, with its split at the nose and both curves round the body, went up and stood connected for the push.

Execution: I used the biggest carry size each trip, which is the cheapest per domino, and timed the loads so the bin was full before it was needed. After the third load I told the table that no more fetching was needed, so nobody wasted time waiting on me. I then used my free hands to inspect the flare join four times (at about 3:45, 4:45, 5:30 and 6:45) and reported what I saw: the first dominoes of the flare sat off the path and needed a nudge or a redo of just those.

Collaboration: I kept my messages short and useful. I gave Jack a specific diagnosis of the join. I also pointed out that Jack and Omar were working on the same spot and suggested one person take it while the other stayed clear, to avoid bumping each other. In the last minute I stayed quiet and hands off so Sofia could finish her final nudge without interference.

Leadership: I took a clear role as the table's supplier and stuck to it. I spotted the doubled-up work at the join and said so directly. I also made the call to stop fetching once the bin was well stocked, and I kept the table's attention on the full-fall check from the nose.

I believe my share of the table's result was about 20 percent. Supply was essential, but the drawing and laying were mostly done by the others.", "my_share_percent": 20}

{"self_assessment": "Impact
I fetched a full load of 40 dominoes for the shared bin early on, so nobody at the table ran short of material. I laid the start domino and traced stroke 1, the top line of the fish, which is the outline from the nose to the upper tail. I then took on the bottom flare at the tail. The start domino is the foundation of the whole fall, and the top line carries about half the body outline.

Execution
I worked in steady batches and traced directly from Sofia's sketch, so the shape stayed true to the plan. I extended the bottom line into the lower flare, restood dominoes that had been knocked, and repeatedly inspected the tail join to find where the chain was off-path. I kept working that area and acted on the advice about the bend into the flare.

Collaboration
I split the work cleanly: I took the top line while Sofia took the bottom line, and Omar helped with the top tail. I said out loud which spot I was working on so people could stay clear of it. I acknowledged Hana's and Sofia's observations and used them, and I thanked Omar for his help on the top tail.

Leadership
I claimed a clear piece of work early and kept the table informed about what I was doing and what I needed from others. I asked for a full check of the fall from the nose. At the end I made sure everyone's hands were off before the push.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I proposed the fish concept in the first minute and sketched it on the pad, with a top line, a bottom line and a flared tail. The design used only gentle curves and a single split at the nose, so one push could run through the whole outline. The finished picture is a clear fish silhouette, and by my trace about 101 of the 108 standing dominoes would fall. I also placed the final dominoes that joined the bottom line into the tail flare, which completed the outline.

Execution: I fetched a tray-load of 12 dominoes and laid the bottom line (stroke 2) from the nose, about 40 dominoes across five build runs, tracing directly from the pad so the curve matched the sketch. I then inspected the nose, the bottom line and the tail join several times to check where the chain was running. At the tail I diagnosed that the bottom line turned into the flare too tightly. I laid the last four dominoes to carry it on and bend it down gently, then called hands-off before the push.

Collaboration: I set up a clear division of labour early. One person took the top line, I took the bottom line, and others handled the bin and the tail. I corrected the start-domino assignment so the right person traced stroke 1. I shared my diagnosis of the join openly, and I stayed clear of other people's work areas to avoid bumps. In the last minutes I called a hands-off so nothing was disturbed before the push.

Leadership: I picked the animal, produced the plan everyone built from, and gave the table a shared checkpoint (check the joins, then the whole fall). I kept the group focused on what would actually fall, and I called the hands-off near the end.

I estimate my share of the table's result at about 30%.", "my_share_percent": 30}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I supplied the material the build ran on. Early on I fetched a full load of 40 dominoes for the shared bin, and the table drew on it for the rest of the session without needing another trip. I also helped the fish read clearly. I stood a domino back up at the nose split so the fall could pass into both the top and bottom lines. I extended the top line into the upper tail flare, laying 13 dominoes in total across a few passes, which helped give the fish its tail.

Execution: I worked in short, targeted bursts rather than starting separate pieces. I fixed the nose fork and carried the top line forward from where it stopped, so everything stayed connected to the run. I inspected the key areas repeatedly (the fork, the top tail, the bottom-to-flare join) to see what the fall would actually reach. At the final check, by eye, nearly all of the standing dominoes were connected to the start. The picture is a fish with a split-tail silhouette.

Collaboration: I kept the table informed with frequent, specific updates about what I was touching and where, and I offered to cover gaps ('shout and I'll close it'). I took on the supporting jobs the table needed, such as the bin supply, the nose fork and the top tail. I stayed clear of other people's work areas near the end, including during the final push, so nothing got bumped.

Leadership: I kept the mood light and the energy up, backed the fish idea quickly so we didn't spend time debating, and made sure the table had what it needed to build. I called for hands-off at the end so the finished picture stayed intact for the push.", "my_share_percent": 25}

{"ratings": {"Omar": {"rating": 5, "why": "Every time I saw him he was reliable: he redirected gracefully, fixed the nose fork, helped with the tail, and offered to close the join. He is the only one with consistent observed contributions and no unfulfilled promises, though I didn't see him on the last visit and his claim that nearly everything connects is unverified."}, "Sofia": {"rating": 3, "why": "She showed the strongest leadership I saw: she took initiative on the join, gave a clear and fair fallback plan, and her bottom line was connected. But when I left, her 'closing now' calls had twice produced no visible result and the flare was still pale, which contradicts her claim that she completed the outline and that about 101 dominoes would fall."}, "Hana": {"rating": 3, "why": "I saw good early coordination at 5:00, and her reports of supplying the bin and diagnosing the flare join are plausible but mostly unverified. I never saw her build, so I'm placing her in the middle until I know more about what she built and what 'bin's still full' meant."}, "Jack": {"rating": 1, "why": "He gave three 'on it' updates on the join (5:15, 5:45, 7:45) with no visible result, and Sofia had to step in at 8:00, which suggests the join had stalled with him. His communication was good and he did build the top line, but execution on the critical join was a miss, and his self-assessment glosses over that."}}}
